content: 1. Efforts should be made to enhance the capacity of individuals and communities to actively participate in leprosy-related services. 2. Communities should be involved in initiatives aimed at improving the quality and accessibility of leprosy services. 3. Coalitions should be formed among individuals affected by leprosy, and these coalitions or their members should be integrated with other community-based organizations to foster collaboration. 4. Programs should be developed to facilitate income generation for individuals affected by leprosy and their families, helping them achieve financial stability. 5. Community-based rehabilitation programs should be supported to address the needs of individuals with disabilities related to leprosy. 6. Efforts should be directed toward abolishing discriminatory laws and promoting inclusive policies that support the integration of individuals affected by leprosy into society. 7. The Global Leprosy Strategy 2016–2020 emphasizes strengthening government ownership, coordination, and partnerships to combat leprosy. 8. The strategy aims to stop the transmission of leprosy, prevent its complications, and eliminate discrimination against those affected by the disease. 9. The ultimate goal is to reduce the global burden of leprosy by 2020 and work toward a leprosy-free world. 10. Early detection of leprosy and prompt treatment are critical to preventing disabilities and reducing the transmission of the infection within communities. 11. The proportion of Grade 2 Disability (G2D) cases among newly diagnosed patients and the G2D rate in a population are key indicators of the effectiveness of early detection efforts. 12. These indicators also reflect the level of awareness about early signs of leprosy, access to leprosy services, and the diagnostic skills of healthcare staff. 13. The strategy envisions a long-term goal of a leprosy-free world, defined as a community free from the morbidity, disabilities, and social consequences associated with leprosy. 14. To achieve this, the strategy focuses on improving early detection, reducing transmission, and minimizing the number of new G2D cases. 15. By 2020, the strategy aims to achieve zero disabilities among newly diagnosed children with leprosy. 16. This will be accomplished through the introduction of a single treatment regimen for all forms of leprosy, targeted case detection in high-endemic areas, and contact screening. 17. The target of zero disability in new pediatric cases highlights the unacceptability of leprosy-related disabilities in children and aims to stimulate community support for the program. 18. Each new pediatric case with G2D should prompt an investigation into the reasons for delayed detection and diagnosis, as well as the development of new approaches to prevent recurrence. 19. Baseline data on G2D among pediatric patients were collected in 2015. 20. The 2013 International Leprosy Summit in Bangkok reaffirmed political commitment to leprosy control, with health ministers from high-endemic countries signing the Bangkok Declaration. 21. The Nippon Foundation has pledged increased funding for leprosy-related activities to support countries in fulfilling their commitments. 22. Individuals affected by leprosy often face stigma and discrimination, which negatively impact their access to diagnosis, treatment outcomes, and societal functioning. 23. Stigma is a significant cause of delayed diagnosis, facilitating the continued transmission of the infection within families and communities. 24. An indicator has been introduced to monitor discrimination against individuals affected by leprosy, along with additional social indicators for program evaluation. 25. The Global Leprosy Strategy 2016–2020 will be discussed in global forums to ensure increased commitment to reducing the disease burden and preventing lifelong disabilities in children affected by leprosy. 26. Over the past three decades, significant progress has been made in leprosy control due to the widespread availability of multidrug therapy (MDT), effective strategies, strong partnerships, and political commitment. 27. Leprosy was eliminated as a public health problem at the global level in 2000, defined as a registered prevalence of less than one case per 10,000 population. 28. More than 16 million patients have been diagnosed and treated since the introduction of MDT. 29. The Final Push to Eliminate Leprosy as a Public Health Problem (2000–2005) successfully engaged policymakers and the public through advocacy, communication, and campaigns. 30. All countries with populations of one million or more have achieved the elimination of leprosy as a public health problem at the national level. 31. However, three countries—India, Brazil, and Indonesia—continue to report more than 10,000 new cases annually, accounting for 81% of newly diagnosed cases globally. 32. Detection of new cases has shown only a modest decline in recent years, and the G2D rate among new cases has remained static. 33. Leprosy interventions must focus on enhancing efforts in high-burden countries to ensure timely case detection and guide countries with smaller case numbers on reducing transmission. 34. WHO will collect data on newly detected pediatric patients with G2D to monitor progress and guide interventions. 35. Challenges in leprosy control include the detection of undiagnosed cases, delayed diagnosis, stigma, social exclusion, and inadequate prevention and care for disabilities. 36. The low proportion of females among new cases in some countries suggests differential access to diagnosis and treatment, requiring systematic data collection disaggregated by sex. 37. Meaningful engagement of all stakeholders, including individuals affected by leprosy and private providers, remains limited. 38. Identification, education, and examination of contacts have been slow and underreported in many countries. 39. Prevention and care for disabilities, especially post-treatment, remain a challenge in most countries. 40. Public apathy toward leprosy and its low priority on political agendas hinder comprehensive efforts to combat the disease. 41. There is a lack of new diagnostic tools, drugs, and knowledge about transmission, as well as inadequate tools to manage complications, necessitating coordinated research efforts. 42. Integration without sustained supervision and monitoring, coupled with reduced funding, has impeded progress and raised concerns about the quality and comparability of leprosy data. 43. The vision of the strategy is a leprosy-free world, with the goal of further reducing the global and local leprosy burden. 44. By 2020, the strategy aims for zero G2D among pediatric patients, a reduction in new G2D cases to less than one per million population, and the elimination of discriminatory legislation. 45. The WHO Global Leprosy Programme will conduct a mid-term evaluation in 2018 to assess progress and review evidence related to chemotherapy and diagnostics. 46. Countries that have not achieved elimination at the subnational level will benefit from the operational guidelines of the Global Strategy for 2016–2020. 47. Key tenets of the strategy include early detection, prompt treatment with a uniform MDT regimen, inclusion of affected individuals, enhanced research, and wider partnerships. 48. A global research agenda will be developed to create new tools for interrupting transmission and reducing disability. 49. National governments bear the primary responsibility for leprosy control and must adopt coordinated approaches involving multiple departments and agencies. 50. Partnerships with international organizations, NGOs, community-based organizations, and affected individuals are essential for sustainability and progress. 51. Cross-border collaboration may be necessary to ensure continuity of care and interrupt transmission. 52. Efforts should focus on sustaining expertise, mobilizing resources, reducing stigma, and promoting community-based rehabilitation. 53. Regional leprosy training centers and e-learning tools should be strengthened to sustain expertise. 54. Nursing and medical school curricula should include leprosy to raise awareness among healthcare workers. 55. Former patients and their families can serve as resources to sustain knowledge about the disease. 56. Social workers and support departments should facilitate societal inclusion for those affected. 57. Quality leprosy services should prioritize children and women, promoting early detection through periodic screening.
